text:
OMAHA, Neb. — Five years ago this fall, Adrian Martinez played his final game in a Nebraska football uniform.

Much has since changed for the quarterback from California, who won a Big 12 championship at Kansas State in 2022 and starred in the United Football League around his time with three NFL teams. The San Francisco 49ers activated Martinez from the practice squad for six weeks last season as the backup to Mac Jones while Brock Purdy managed an injury. Martinez re-signed in January with the Niners.

He’s back in Nebraska now. Martinez is working in the lead-up to training camp alongside rookie quarterback Cole Payton of the Philadelphia Eagles, a fifth-round pick out of North Dakota State. Martinez and Payton throw three times a week to eager high school and college receivers under the direction of QB trainer John Teigland. Two NFL quarterbacks stand out here against the backdrop of summer in suburbia.

“It’s simpler than it’s made out to be sometimes,” Martinez said. “You go lift weights, run, throw, study, prepare. Omaha is as good a place as any for that.”

Martinez married a Nebraskan last summer. He and his wife, Marisa, settled in the Omaha area, and he made an effort this year to give back. Martinez recently spoke to the football players at Gretna East High about his experiences in dealing with injuries and other adversity. He stood on a stage in the high school theater and captured the attention of the kids.

“They were dialed in and focused,” Gretna East coach Justin Haberman said. “He was electric. The best thing is, he related to the kids, because he went through struggles.”

Martinez refused to take payment. He fielded questions and dodged nothing, Haberman said, handling every answer with class. In 2021 and throughout his career at Nebraska, Martinez endured criticism from fans and media members who did not know the extent of his injuries. He played much of that final season with a broken jaw.

He left the school after four years as a starter with a school-record 10,792 yards of total offense.

At 26, Martinez remains gracious toward Nebraska.

He and Payton have worked out several times at Gretna East this summer. They throw to Haberman’s receivers, explaining the purpose of drills for the high school coaches and players to absorb. On Tuesday afternoon this week, they trained in the heat on the turf at Omaha Westside, Payton’s alma mater.

“I’m not asking a high school kid to run a 10- to 12-yard out at the same pace as Mike Evans,” Martinez said. “But I think they enjoy catching NFL balls. There are a lot of kids here who want to play at the next level. It’s cool to integrate myself into that.”

His pairing with Payton just made sense, Martinez said. Payton won two FCS national championships at North Dakota State and led the Bison to a perfect regular season last year. He was a finalist for the Walter Payton Award.

Payton recently returned from Orlando, Fla., and a series of throwing sessions with Jalen Hurts, who organized the trip for the Eagles’ quarterbacks, wide receivers and tight ends. He leaves again next week for camp in Philadelphia.

He’ll take Martinez’s wisdom with him. Martinez shared his knowledge from a pro career he began as an undrafted free agent with the Detroit Lions in 2023. The Lions cut Martinez in August of that year. Birmingham of the UFL signed him. He was named MVP of the league championship in June 2024 and signed with the New York Jets in July 2024.

Martinez stuck on the Jets’ practice squad in 2024. San Francisco signed him early last season. He finally made his NFL debut in Week 9 against the New York Giants after Jones subbed himself out in the final seconds of a 34-24 win.

“He’s been doing it the hard way,” Payton said. “It hasn’t been easy. That’s what he brings.”

Payton, 6 feet 3 and 230 pounds, looks to follow former NDSU quarterbacks Carson Wentz, Trey Lance, Easton Stick (another Omahan) and Cam Miller to an NFL career. The Eagles signed Payton to a four-year, $4.6 million rookie deal, but he must make the team to get paid.

Hurts and Andy Dalton are the veteran quarterbacks in Philly, along with third-year pro Tanner McKee out of Stanford.

“What I’ve learned is that I belong,” Payton said. “I was able to train with some big names, go to the Senior Bowl, go to the combine. That gave me a lot of confidence. I know I can do it better than a lot of those guys.”

Payton, 23, impressed Martinez.

“Being a quarterback in the NFL is a unique experience,” Martinez said. “Anything that I can impart on him, I definitely will. But I think he’s got a pretty good grip on things. He’s very accomplished. It’s more about him pushing me.”

Martinez enters camp this month in Santa Clara, Calif., competing for a spot on a roster, too. Second-year quarterback Kurtis Rourke is healthy after missing much of 2025 with a knee injury. He was a seventh-round draft pick last year out of Indiana. Purdy and Jones return, too.

The Niners figure to keep Rourke or Martinez behind the top two.

A home base in Omaha — and the relationships Martinez has established — have helped keep him grounded amid the NFL pressure.

“It’s cliche, but get comfortable being uncomfortable,” he said. “I’ve had plenty of quarterback battles and competitions throughout my career. There’s the understanding that every year, you’re going to fight. If you want to be in this thing, you have to work. You have to be willing to compete and be willing to fail and learn and understand it’s a process. It’s not about surviving the first day of training camp. It’s the collective effort that will get you over the hump.”

text:
Los Angeles Dodgers designated hitter/starting pitcher Shohei Ohtani has had a complicated last month in regards to his knee.

The superstar quickly emerged as a frontrunner for the Cy Young award and currently has a 1.79 ERA through 14 starts on the mound. Ahead of what was going to be his 15th start of the season, Ohtani was scratched six hours before first pitch due to "continued irritation in his left knee. He also missed the All-Star Game to rest and receive treatment.

The saga started when Ohtani left a mid-June game early with what was later diagnosed as knee inflammation. After missing just one contest, the four-time MVP's returned and hit a leadoff solo home run. As time would reveal, the problem existed more on the pitching side of things.

Dodgers pitching coach Mark Prior recently shared his concern level with the Los Angeles Times' Maddie Lee regarding Ohtani's recent knee complications.

“I would say, moderately concerned,” Prior said. “But no more concerned than I probably am with anybody else who’s had to deal with aches and pains. Hopefully, this break and this rest will get it to calm down a little bit, and then we’ll see where we’re at next weekend.”

Prior touched on what he thinks the actual issue is, and echoed what Ohtani previously noted in the belief that his mechanics may lay at the root of the problem.

“I think we’ve identified the issue,” Prior said. “Sometimes the fix isn’t always the easiest, especially with a guy who doesn’t spend probably the same amount of time on the mechanics of it.”

Back in 2019, Ohtani required surgery to address bipartite patella, an uncommon congenital condition where the two bones of his knee cap failed to fuse. He wasn't sure if there is any connection between his current and past knee issues.

Manager Dave Roberts recently spoke on Ohtani's knee treatment and confirmed that fluid was drained but no injection was given.

As for this weekend's series against the New York Yankees, he said that Ohtani will be in the starting lineup. On Thursday, it was announced that he will not be pitching in the Bronx.

Ohtani is well on his way to earning his fifth MVP award this season, but will likely fall short of his Cy Young goals. His health is the most important part of his game at this point in the season, and though accolades are nice, October success is likely the only way Ohtani wants to end the 2026 campaign.

title: Does Joe Burrow get dinged too much for injury history? Dehner Jr. Bengals mailbag

— Sean C. This will always be the quiet asterisk to every talented Bengals roster until time heals all wounds, quite literally, in the Burrow conversation.
Yes, they can be largely unlucky, but there are players who are just injury-prone (I am not putting that label specifically on Burrow!)
That said, the ideal scenario for the Bengals involves Turner under contract for the foreseeable future.
Of the current Bengals players and coaches, who has the yap to cut a good heel or babyface pro wrestling promo?
text:
We are merely 12 days away from the first practice of training camp and I can already taste the cow brains in the mock turtle soup.

We’ve nearly made it, people.

As the fan survey showed, there’s as much excitement for this year as for any in a long time, and I’ve felt that from your anticipation over the last month. Or maybe it’s just the wild overreaction to the Dexter Lawrence workout video. Either way, there’s no doubt Bengals fans can’t wait to overreact to every training camp play given how high the hopes are for this year.

On that note, the questions had a more concerning tone at some points than I expected, but we all need a little yin to our yang, so let’s do it.

(Questions have been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.)

I’m curious as to your thoughts on Joe Burrow’s accountability for playing a part in the failure of last season. Of course, the defense was terrible. As a fan, it was still frustrating to hear some of his comments after losses.

You know what’s fun? Not throwing back-to-back picks deep in your own territory in Buffalo with a lead. You know what gets laughs? Not getting shut out at home against a divisional opponent with your season on the line. You know what’s a barrel of monkeys? Being on the field.

Do you think I’m justified in feeling that way at times? Or am I being too cynical, and I should just shut up and enjoy a QB with this much talent? — Sean C.

This will always be the quiet asterisk to every talented Bengals roster until time heals all wounds, quite literally, in the Burrow conversation.

This came up last week in the middle of the quarterback ranking madness that took over the shouty shows. And, I can’t believe I’m going to say this, but Bart Scott made a valid point. The reason Burrow ranks fourth is that availability is a factor. It just has to be. Yes, they can be largely unlucky, but there are players who are just injury-prone (I am not putting that label specifically on Burrow!) and it ends up following them, and eventually dooms their careers. I think of Tyler Eifert and John Ross among recent Bengals examples. Quarterbacks such as Sam Bradford and Matthew Stafford battled the label for a while. Even back to Michael Vick and Chad Pennington.

Burrow’s injury list is long now, so you have to factor it into the rest of his elite profile. Appendix, calf, ACL, another knee, throat, wrist, toe, finger. He broke his hand at Ohio State. Even in his biggest games, injuries were a part of the moment. He tore cartilage in his ribs in the national title game and sprained his MCL in the Super Bowl.

I don’t think Burrow has ever run from this reality. He’s done work every offseason with the idea of sustaining a full season and becoming durable. I think all of that came to a head during the two months he missed after turf toe surgery last year and he went into deeply philosophical thought, running himself through the wringer emotionally.

This is not a lack of accountability or a lack of work toward healthier seasons. It’s just football, and the flukiness of so many of his injuries is what makes it so concerning. You can limit the hits, call quick game and not even be playing and still have to worry about a toe or wrist ligament snapping or an appendix bursting.

Burrow could easily follow Stafford’s path and turn those early injury-prone whispers into a Hall of Fame career where the early injuries are a mere footnote. No question. And I do not question his awareness and approach to the issue. It’s just part of his story right now until it isn’t. It’s perfectly understandable for that to be reflected in how he’s viewed.

The Bengals and this city still shouldn’t trade him for another quarterback on the planet. Both things can be true.

Do you think the Bengals have been in touch with any teams about trading for a linebacker? It seems that with the draft behind us and the free-agency well run dry, that is the only available option. It would seem to me to be a sensible use of future draft capital. — Ed M.

Why haven’t the Bengals signed a veteran LB and swing tackle yet? For depth/backup/injury insurance at least. Camp is a week away! — Mike D.

I guess my biggest questions going into training camp are: do you think the Bengals are going to address some obvious weaknesses? For all the talk of linebacker, and I get it, I think the lack of a swing tackle and starting nickelback is much bigger issues. Do you think they will sign someone of any quality to either of these positions? — Ryan C.

Ed, Mike and Ryan, congrats, you hit on the most popular topic in this week’s mailbag. You aren’t wrong; all of those positions could use a veteran insurance policy for depth or competition. I’d currently rank them cornerback, linebacker, swing tackle. But all are on the same priority tier to canvass the league for options. You could arguably throw running back in there, but I’m comfortable with the Chase Brown-Samaje Perine-Tahj Brooks trio at the top.

I do think another move is coming. That could be a trade in the Billy Price-B.J. Hill mold, where one of the odd men out on the defensive line fetches a veteran linebacker or corner.

They successfully added last year, signing Noah Fant and Dalton Risner during camp, who both contributed during the season, then trading for Joe Flacco. They’ve made deals to fill gaps before, even going back to the 2010 fleecing of the Jaguars, exchanging David Jones for Reggie Nelson.

The biggest variable is how the current options look in camp. If Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight struggle or get injured, yeah, they will amp up the aggressiveness at those spots. The same can be said for swing tackle Cody Ford and the battle royale in the back of the corner room.

The Bengals’ strategy seems to be to see how things play out in their camp — as well as other teams getting more desperate about their needs — and see if partners emerge. That, along with an intriguing list of available free agents, makes me think an important contributor or two for 2026 is not yet on the roster.

Al Golden has described the “Viper” as an edge defender who can set the edge, rush the passer and drop into coverage. With Boye Mafe and Cashius Howell now providing natural fits for that role, and Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight entering Year 2 after extensive rookie experience, how much more multiplicity can Golden build into the defense, and what changes should we expect in the fronts, pressures and coverages he uses? — Harold S.

You are exactly right; Golden finally has the pieces he wanted to make his defense work. It reminds me of the 2021 Bengals finally giving Lou Anarumo the types of players he needed, and his game-planning skills as a coordinator started to shine.

We don’t know if that will happen with Golden, but we do know he wanted players like Mafe and Howell in his scheme and didn’t have them last year. Hence, you’d see Joseph Ossai or Myles Murphy 15 yards downfield far too often and looking silly because of it.

Bringing the “Viper” position to life will give them versatility without substitution, morphing from a 4-3 to a 3-4 in a single shift and having the players to execute it. Plus, the general havoc expected to be created by the defensive line along with familiarity of the system in Year 2 makes everyone a step better.

Golden made it clear most of last year he was attempting to run the simplest version of his defense imaginable because that’s what that young group required. He was limited. That won’t be the case this year, so yes, he will be more exotic and multiple. That is the expectation because the players can handle it this time around.

Is Chase Brown a member of the Bengals in 2027? — Anonymous

Let’s talk contracts, ’tis the season. Yes, I believe Brown will be a member of the Bengals in 2027. First off, what’s not to love about Brown’s game and place in this offense? He’s become a centerpiece of what they do and has challenged Ja’Marr Chase consistently for most scrimmage yards each season.

They don’t have anything resembling a transition candidate on the roster, which is their style in populating that position. Maybe Brooks will show more in Year 2, but a more aggressive draft pick would make me think they are considering moving on.

They can franchise tag him if they can’t agree. The RB tag is digestible. Running backs were tagged at one year and $14.3 million in 2026, the second-lowest-paid position, only topping specialists. That speaks the Bengals’ language as they continue to work on a potential longer deal for him.

He might even sign a deal before this season, but that would largely be dependent on negotiations with the other three prime candidates.

There’s a lot of chatter about extensions, particularly DJ Turner. Besides Turner, who else do you think is getting an extension this summer? Myles Murphy, Dax Hill, Chase Brown, Jordan Battle? —Michael P.

The smart money is on Turner because he’s the best player of the bunch. His agent also represents Dax Hill and Joey Porter Jr. (the agent also recently changed employers from Athletes First to Win Sports Group). All three of these deals could impact the others, but the Bengals would start by targeting Turner before moving that money elsewhere.

That very well could happen; if they can’t find a deal with Turner, for example, they could then turn to Myles Murphy with a sweeter deal than previously offered. Or Brown or Hill. You get the point. It’s just a complicated case of who is willing to accept the offer on the table and who is comfortable betting on himself. Players go different ways with this topic every season, so we’ll see how it plays out in this case. That said, the ideal scenario for the Bengals involves Turner under contract for the foreseeable future.

Season ticket holder from Atlanta. I went to the All Access event in June (it was a lot of fun!). I noticed a ton of stadium updates still in process. How are the renovations going? Any rumblings that they will not be done before the season starts? — Carl O.

Although every home construction project in the greater Cincinnati area appears to be behind, the Bengals are rolling on schedule. The Cincinnati Music Festival is next weekend, and the projects in Phase One of the renovations in the new lease are substantially done. All systems go for 2026. The renovations are the most extensive since Paycor Stadium opened in 2000. I’d look to hear more about all that in the coming days and weeks.

Of the current Bengals players and coaches, who has the yap to cut a good heel or babyface pro wrestling promo? Feel free to offer several people if you wish to do so. — Ed H.

All right, Ed, this is what I’m talking about. It’s July, for goodness sake. Frankly, I’m disappointed in how many of you were asking real questions about transactions and renovations. Let’s talk wrestling promo candidates.

Here’s my list:

1. Ted Karras

2.

3.

4.

5.

6.

7. Orlando Brown Jr.

8-Ja’Marr Chase

Karras basically already does this after games, win or lose. His intensity, inflection, delivery and general caricature of a football animal make him the ideal answer. Did we forget 2022 in Tennessee? The closest thing to a real WWE post-match moment the NFL has witnessed this decade. Legend status.

Sidenote: Orlando has the charisma and size. I could see it. Lastly, if Ja’Marr could channel his trash talk on the field into his often animated postgame news conferences, he’d have a chance at a mean promo.

But, no, the answer to this is Karras, and anybody who fights me on that, well, as Karras said to Titans fans: Right up yours.

text:
Tennessee basketball forward Christian Fermin will miss the remainder of summer practice because of a fractured left hand, GoVols247 learned Thursday from a source with direct knowledge of the situation.

The redshirt senior who transferred from VCU this offseason underwent surgery Thursday to repair the fracture. Fermin is expected to miss 4-6 weeks. Tennessee is not concerned about his long-term status.

Fermin fractured his left hand during a drill in practice on Monday. Trainer Chad Newman immediately assisted Fermin off the floor while holding his left hand. Fermin returned to the sideline later in practice with his hand in a brace.

Tennessee is scheduled to conclude summer practice July 30.

Fermin was the last addition for Tennessee from the transfer portal this offseason. The forward committed May 14 to give the Vols an eight-man transfer class that 247Sports ranks No. 2 in the country.

"It's been hard," Fermin told the media July 7 about his first with Tennessee. "There's a standard here of just how much work you're going to put in every day, and I feel like it's definitely far beyond my college experience so far, as far as just the amount of work we're putting in and just the intensity in it. So I'll say it's just full of work, just hard work."

He played in just four games for the Rams last season due to a personal matter, but played in 86 games the three seasons prior. Fermin appeared in 34 games as a junior in 2024-25 to average 4.6 points and 3.1 rebounds in 19.4. minutes per game. His 1.4 blocks per game were second-best on the the team, as he finished with 47 blocks.

Fermin scored a season-high 14 points against Loyola and had a 12-point game against Boston College, and his best all-around game came against La Salle (seven points, eight rebounds and five blocked shots).

"Here (at Tennessee), everything is really just based upon just being where you have to be and being consistent and giving your all," Fermin said. "I would just say that I think there's a lot of structure here, so I feel like that's definitely something that you can gain from being here, is just structurally you're going to be on point. You're gonna learn how to be punctual and everything, and yeah, just definitely I would say just a lot of balance and structure has been given to me just coming here."

Fermin started all 38 games as a sophomore in 2023-24 to average 5.2 points and 4.0 rebounds in 21.4 minutes per game. He shot 57% overall and blocked a team-high 55 shots, while finishing in double figures six times.

His first career double-double came in a win against Samford. He added a season-high five blocks, and also had a 14-rebound game against George Washington.

Fermin appeared in 14 games off the bench as a freshman to average 0.4 points and 0.7 rebounds in 3.4 minutes.

text:
Last year around this time, every expectation on the Patriots revolved around getting back to respectability.

Following a five-year-long fiasco that involved the departure of Tom Brady, the unceremonious end to Bill Belichick's tenure, the Cam Newton/Mac Jones/Bailey Zappe quarterback carousel, back-to-back 4-13 seasons and the brief-but-disastrous head coaching campaign from Jerod Mayo, most Patriots fans would have been overjoyed to just see the Patriots go 9-8, remain in contention for a wild-card spot through Christmas, and take an important first step back toward NFL relevance.

Instead, they witnessed one of the great turnarounds in sports history, with the Patriots going 14-3, winning their division for the first time in six years and improbably reaching the Super Bowl.

Now, to say the least, expectations have been raised.

Naturally, high expectations bring pressure on everyone to live up to the new standards. And while every single player, coach and staff member in the NFL feels pressure to perform on a daily basis, here's a countdown of the Patriots facing the most pressure ahead of training camp opening next weekend in Foxboro.

8. Gabe Jacas

Had the rookie EDGE simply been a second-round draft pick who signed his contract and showed up to work, he likely wouldn't land on this list. But Jacas' first few months as a pro have been a bit rocky.

Head coach Mike Vrabel revealed during minicamp that he had not spent any time on a football field with Jacas, stating that the 22-year-old had a "procedure" while giving no further explanation.

The Patriots traded up to draft Jacas at 55th overall (sending a fourth-round pick and a sixth-round pick to the Chargers in addition to their original pick at No. 63). He's yet to sign his rookie deal, he's yet to take the field due to a lingering injury that the Patriots may or may not have fully known about, and he was drafted to fill a significant need for the team (the Patriots ranked 26th in sacks and 24th in pressure rate). There's a lot stacked up for the rookie.

7. Harold Landry

Keeping it on the edge, the veteran Landry came out of the gates hot last year, racking up 5.5 sacks and 12 total QB hits in his first seven games with the Patriots, looking like a solid "Vrabel Guy" addition. But he was slowed significantly in the second half of the season, first appearing on the injury report in Week 7 with an ankle issue. He dealt with a knee injury later in the year, keeping him off the field for the final two regular-season games and the AFC Championship Game.

In the three playoff games he did participate in, Landry touched the quarterback just once while taking only 51 snaps. He was a complete non-factor.

K'Lavon Chaisson (7.5 sacks) got a payday in D.C., replaced in free agency by Dre'Mont Jones, who's not expected to serve in a pure pass rusher role. And with the aforementioned Jacas situation, the Patriots kind of need Landry to be that first-half version of himself for the entire year. But his 2026 got off to a rough start, as he was not participating in spring practice.

"Harold has played a lot of football, and so we just have to try to -- this is all part of everyone has a little different plan," Vrabel said in June regarding the 30-year-old Landry. "For him to take reps right now in the spring, I feel like is unnecessary. We will just keep working to make sure that he is ready to go when we need him."

A football coach saying it's "unncessary" for a player to participate in practice is almost unheard of, so Vrabel's comment was worth a raised eyebrow or two.

At some point this summer, Landry's going to have to practice. And if he still doesn't look right, he and the Patriots are going to have some problems.

6. Christian Gonzalez

The sorta-kinda-not-really hold-in during minicamp wasn't a significant issue. Veteran cornerbacks aren't getting overloaded with scheme and strategy during spring sessions, so Christian Gonzalez mostly just missed out on a little bit of exercise.

But come training camp, the stakes will be raised.

And whether Gonzalez gets his big-money extension (he should) or holds out until reaching some resolution, he's obviously going to invite a lot of attention on himself.

Frankly, he'd be higher on the list, but there's little doubt that the 24-year-old can maintain his elite level of play. His pressure is more about the stress and uncertainty that can accompany a drawn-out negotiation.

5. Hunter Henry

Hunter Henry has been as consistent a player as there can possibly be during his time with the Patriots, playing in 86 of a possible 90 games since 2021. He's averaged a tick under 76 percent of the team's offensive snaps during that time, in the top three of target leaders every season.

The pressure on Henry isn't about performance, per se. It's simply about staying on the field.

With Austin Hooper gone and free agent signee Julian Hill injured, the Patriots only have rookie Eli Raridon behind him on the depth chart (though tight end-turned-fullback Jack Westover could move back into the position, too).

Henry has always had a Hooper (2024-25), Mike Gesicki (2023) or Jonnu Smith (2021-22) to help ease the load a bit at the position, but won't have anything close to that kind of luxury this year. Set to turn 32 in December, there is simply a lot resting on Henry's shoulders.

4. A.J. Brown

It's difficult to think of any Patriots acquisition in the 21st century who's been looked at as a savior the way A.J. Brown has. He's not a worthwhile gamble on a depressed asset; he's a major investment who's expected to reshape the entire offense. (Drew Bledsoe, as the No. 1 pick back in 1993, comes to mind as the only comparison.)

With that, obviously, comes tremendous responsibility for Brown, who celebrated his 29th birthday at the end of June.

Brown caught 78 passes for 1,003 yards and seven touchdowns for Philadelphia last season -- an objectively good season. If he does the same thing in 2026, people around New England will be massively disappointed.

There's little doubt that Brown can hit the 1,000-yard mark, but New England fans are likely hoping to see the Brown from 2022 and 2023, when he averaged nearly 1,500 yards and nine touchdowns per season. Meanwhile, Philly fans (and, frankly, fans of 30 other teams) are hoping that the whispers about Brown's deteriorating knees are true, and that he'll be a bust for the Patriots.

Being realistic, the 1,400-yard days are likely over for Brown, but you understand the point. The trading away of a first-round pick is a big deal, and with everybody hoping for Drake Maye to maintain an MVP-caliber performance, the bulk of that responsibility is going to fall on the new No. 1 receiver.

3. Will Campbell

Before suffering a knee injury in Week 12 in Cincinnati, Will Campbell was a pretty good NFL left tackle. Not great, not an All-Pro. But pretty good. Fine. Not a problem.

When he returned for the final regular-season game and the playoff run, he was ... bad. Really bad. Outside of the AFC title game in Denver, Campbell was a consistent problem on the left side of the line, getting overpowered on bull rushes and getting beaten to the edge on speed rushes. Khalil Mack got the better of him, Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter had him in a blender, and in a Super Bowl when the entire offensive line played poorly, Campbell arguably played the worst. (PFF gave him a 38.3 grade for that game. Nobody else on the line got worse than a 52.3 grade.)

Vrabel expressed confidence in Campbell after that brutal Super Bowl showing, saying, "He's our left tackle, he'll get better, he'll get stronger." Vrabel also went out and traded up to draft left tackle Caleb Lomu in the first round of the ensuing draft.

Actions. Words. You know the drill.

Campbell will enter camp as the starting left tackle. Lomu will get a ton of reps on the right side, given Morgan Moses' veteran workload. This will not be a day-to-day story throughout camp.

But when the season begins, fairly or unfairly, Campbell's going to have millions of sets of eyeballs homed in on his every step and every mistake. He entered the league surrounded by questions about whether or not he had the physical tools to be an NFL left tackle. They haven't gone away after a year in the league, and it's up to him to try to silence them.

2. Drake Maye

If you were to fire up a classic top-eight list of players facing the most pressure on every NFL team, the quarterback would likely land in the top one or two spots for just about all of them. Such is life in the NFL. The quarterback gets all the credit for success and all the blame for failures, and there's really no way around it.

For Maye, certain aspects of his marvelous 2025 campaign are simply unsustainable. The 72 percent completion rate, for one. The 113.5 passer rating and 77.1 QBR, for two more. The 8.9 yards-per-attempt average for another. Even the 1.6 percent interception rate showed that Maye had a little bit of luck on his side over the course of the 2025 season, especially considering the number of tight-window passes and deep shots he took all year.

The efficiency Maye had passing the ball was on another level last year, and it would be unreasonable to expect those numbers to even stay close to last year's.

But can Maye throw more than 31 touchdowns? He better. Can he finish higher than fourth in receiving yards now that he has a legitimate No. 1 to throw to? He should. And after a year of learning what Josh McDaniels and Mike Vrabel wanted him to do and not to do while running the football, can he take a leap forward as a rusher after running for 450 yards and four touchdowns? You've got to believe it.

Maye has been compared to Josh Allen from some of his first starts in the league, so Allen's third-year leap (going from 3,089 yards and 20 touchdowns to 4,544 yards and 37 touchdowns) will surely be used as a desired path for Maye this coming season. (Allen was 24 years old that season in 2020, and Maye will turn 2024 in late August, if you're looking for a parallel.)

Maye is still not in a perfect system, but nobody is. What he does have is a team that beefed up its offensive line, spending big free-agent money (Alijah Vera-Tucker this year, Moses and Garrett Bradbury a year ago) and draft capital (Lomu, Campbell, Jared Wilson) to protect him while also landing the bona fide No. 1 receiver in Brown. Working with the same offensive coordinator for a second consecutive year (something Maye hasn't done since high school) should be the ideal setup as he tries to build on a breakout year.

The pieces are in place for Maye to be even better than he was a year ago. He should make the leap. If he doesn't, whether it's his fault or not, everybody will rush in to declare last year a fluke.

1. Mike Vrabel

The proverbial honeymoon is over.

As noted already, the hope last year was that Vrabel -- a no-nonsense, straightforward, wise football man -- could reinhabit Gillette Stadium and deliver a level of respectability to the operation. He did that in spades.

But following a Super Bowl where he was clearly outcoached, an offseason of constant tabloid reporting on his personal life followed. The actual impact of that "scandal" on the football team can be debated, but it nevertheless took the shine off a pristine first season at the helm for the New England franchise.

Now in 2026, the schedule gets harder. A lot harder.

Now in 2026, the Patriots will not have the element of surprise. Just like in the glory days, the reigning AFC champs are sure to get every opponent's best shot each week.

Now in 2026, the head coach is expected to maintain a standard of winning that he helped to establish last year.

The job wasn't easy last year, but it's a lot harder this year. And with an NFL public waiting to sling some arrows at last year's NFL Coach of the Year for any and every misstep, Vrabel will have to apply a laser-like focus on the task at hand on a daily basis and impart that mindset to the entire staff and roster each and every week.

text:
The Arizona Diamondbacks are back at Chase Field, with the All-Star Break nearly over.

Just like the majority of major league baseball, the Diamondbacks are dealing with their fair share of injuries at the moment. Here's all the latest from manager Torey Lovullo's Thursday media session.

Zac Gallen awaiting second opinions on elbow injury

Struggling right-hander Zac Gallen is dealing with right elbow inflammation.

He was sent back to Arizona prior to the end of the D-backs' recent road trip, and has since been placed on the 15-day injured list.

Elbow inflammation, as long-time fans well know, can be the sign of a more minor absence or a potentially season-ending injury, depending on the diagnosis.

According to Lovullo, Gallen is waiting on second opinions. There was no official diagnosis update.

"Gallen, we're continuing to evaluate," Lovullo said. "He is waiting for other opinions from other doctors. So we'll just keep putting that off until we get everything complete."

Second opinions are often an inauspicious sign. That very process sometimes indicates a more serious injury can be the case, though it is certainly not a guarantee Gallen is destined for Tommy John surgery or anything similar.

Tommy Troy placed on IL with shoulder injury

Outfielder Tommy Troy was recently placed on the IL as well, suffering a right AC joint sprain in his shoulder after making a spectacular catch at the wall in Dodger Stadium. Lovullo did not sound overly concerned about a long-term absence for Troy, but could not offer a specific timeline or grade.

"I have not heard a grade on it. I don't know what that number is," Lovullo said. "I'm hoping it's as short a stint as possible. Does that mean 10 days? I'm hopeful.

"We're just talking about limited range of motion, a little bit of discomfort when he raises his arm. So we've got to get that back, and I've heard that that's improving rapidly."

Troy's IL stint is backdated to July 12, so he could return as early as July 22, though AC joint sprains can eat up weeks to months' worth of recovery depending on the severity.

Other Diamondbacks health updates

Geraldo Perdomo

Fans were understandably unnerved when shortstop Geraldo Perdomo was seen with a wrap on his left hand on Instagram. Lovullo said Perdomo received a cortisone shot to address a nagging issue that arose during Arizona's series in San Diego, but did not sound worried.

"He battles hand issues throughout the course of the year, ever since we've had him," Lovullo said. "I was told it's not going to hinder him whatsoever."

Michael Soroka

Right-hander Michael Soroka (glute strain) threw a bullpen Tuesday. He is not expected back immediately after the break, but that timeline being extended is glute-related, and not a result of any new arm or shoulder issues, Lovullo said. Soroka will likely make a rehab start before returning, though his timeline is somewhat up in the air.

Corbin Burnes and Justin Martinez

Right-hander Corbin Burnes (Tommy John rehab/Teres Major strain) had a follow-up MRI on July 10, which showed positive healing. He has since re-started his throwing program.

Right-hander Justin Martinez (Tommy John rehab) is expected to throw to live hitters soon.

"Martinez is just about to step onto a mound in live," Lovullo said. "I don't know the exact day when he's going to face his lives, but he's very close, very close."

Jordan Lawlar, Ryne Nelson and A.J. Puk

Outfielder Jordan Lawlar (hamstring strain) is progressing well and beginning to ramp up his running and baseball activities. Lovullo said he is "in a good spot." There is no timeline for his return, yet. He will get re-imaged on Friday.

Right-hander Ryne Nelson (elbow strain) and left-hander A.J. Puk (elbow rehab/shoulder setback) are also expected to have follow-up MRIs Friday.

text:
As the Cardinals head toward training camp, azcardinals.com takes a look at each position on the roster before report day. Next up, cornerback.

THE ROOM: Denzel Burke, Kei'Trel Clark, Elijah Culp, Jaden Davis, Will Johnson, Elijah Jones, Kalen King, Max Melton, Sean Murphy-Bunting, Starling Thomas V, Garrett Williams

WHO COULD SEE THE FIELD ON GAME DAY: Will Johnson, Denzel Burke, Garrett Williams, Starling Thomas V, Sean Murphy-Bunting, Max Melton

The Cardinals have spent a lot of high-end draft capital on the position the past few years: Seven of the corners on the roster were drafted by Arizona, four in the second and third rounds. You build for success, you build for depth. Johnson played well enough last season to show why he should be a quality second-round choice. Burke, a fifth-rounder, came out of nowhere to earn a starting job and was effective in carving out that role. But what happens when Williams and Thomas finally are able to play after serious injuries? How does Murphy-Bunting fit in after missing all of last season? These are the things that get sorted out in training camp.

PLAYER IN THE SPOTLIGHT: Max Melton

Johnson is a second rounder that seems to have hit. The Cardinals are still trying to find that with Melton, a second-round selection that has been excellent on special teams but has yet to find consistent footing on defense. Melton's athleticism is evident. He was drafted where he was for a reason. But he faces the inevitable comparisons with the other three cornerbacks drafted right in front of him (Cooper DeJean, Kool-Aid McKinstry, Kamari Lassiter) and a crowded depth chart in his own room to find a bigger role.

PLAYER TO KEEP AN EYE ON: Garrett Williams

Williams tore his Achilles in December. That's an injury that usually waylays a guy for nearly a year. But coach Mike LaFleur said Williams might actually have a chance to play Week 1 against the Chargers, which would be a remarkable recovery – and it would also make the decisions of who will play and when that much more tangled. It would be an excellent development, however; Williams has played well when healthy and for all the injuries the Cardinals have suffered since last year, good injury news would be welcome.

text:
You're not alone if you've never thought about San Francisco 49ers cornerback Jakob Robinson.

The 2025 undrafted free agent out of BYU was signed by the Niners after that year's NFL Draft, yet his rookie year was wiped out by an injury during the preseason that landed him on injured reserve. Although one could argue that was modestly beneficial, given it preserved the original three-year contract he signed with the club.

Unfortunately for Robinson, the context surrounding his already-slim chances of making San Francisco's 53-man roster are tougher this year than they would've been an offseason ago. The 49ers added several cornerbacks over the spring, including veterans like Nate Hobbs and Jack Jones, while also drafting rookie Ephesians Prysock. Those names, among others, are competing against the presumed starting trio of Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green and Upton Stout.

Speaking of Stout, who has the nickel spot all but locked up entering 2026, the Niners potentially envision Robinson as a would-be reserve. After all, both players' frames are similar—Stout is 5-foot-9 and 181 pounds, while Robinson is 5-foot-10 and the same weight.

Yet Robinson likely isn't even sniffing the primary backup job behind Stout entering training camp, and it'd take one major X-factor to allow the second-year pro to even have a chance at making the regular-season squad.

Jakob Robinson must bank on training camp injuries to make 49ers' 53-man roster

Players may openly never say it, but one can't help wonder if a fringe name like Robinson would be OK if someone above him on the depth chart suffered some kind of injury during training camp or in the preseason.

Losing Stout to such would be disastrous, yes. But San Francisco's pickups of players like Hobbs and Jones alleviate that concern. Likewise, other fringe names like Derrick Canteen and Patrick McMorris are in the same predicament as Robinson: banking on said depth chart being tested, due to injuries.

For Robinson, who couldn't see any regular-season action his rookie year but is banking on his 11 interceptions and 21 passes broken up during his four-year BYU tenure as difference makers, the challenge will be getting any substantial field time to impress the 49ers coaching staff.

Barring injury, it'll likely be limited. And even if Robinson does impress modestly enough, it'll be exceptionally difficult for him to overtake the many better-established names ahead of him on the roster.

What'll likely transpire is Robinson seeing field time late in preseason games before a seemingly inevitable pre-Week 1 cut; landing on the practice squad might be a best-case outcome.

title: Phillies' bullpen under further pressure with Brad Keller done for season. What now?
authors: Matt Gelb, Jayne Orenstein, Rebecca Tauber and more
description:
There is a good argument that bullpen reinforcements are the club’s greatest need, despite holes in the outfield and rotation.
Even if the Phillies make a deadline acquisition, several of their current relievers have to assume a more important role.
That is a tactic Dombrowski has often taken at the deadline, the Duran deal being an exception.
Even further back, another two-year deal to setup man Mike Adams was derailed by a significant shoulder injury.
The Phillies were burned by one-year deals to Jordan Romano and Joe Ross last season.
text:
PHILADELPHIA — The day after Brad Keller returned from the injured list, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly saw his highest-paid reliever in the weight room at Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati. Keller was struggling.

“I could tell,” Mattingly said.

The team’s worst fears were realized over the All-Star break when an MRI confirmed that Keller had torn the ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow. His season is over. The Phillies signed Keller to a two-year, $22 million contract, and that deal might yield only 31 1/3 innings of inconsistent relief work because surgery could keep Keller out for most of 2027 as well.

The injury has major ramifications for how the Phillies will approach the Aug. 3 trade deadline. They have one of the best closers in baseball in Jhoan Duran, and an uncertain bridge to him. There is a good argument that bullpen reinforcements are the club’s greatest need, despite holes in the outfield and rotation.

“With the team in the position that we’re in, you want to come in the second half and fight with the boys,” Keller said. “Just tough to swallow this pill right now.”

For now, a greater focus shifts to José Alvarado, Orion Kerkering and Jonathan Bowlan. Even if the Phillies make a deadline acquisition, several of their current relievers have to assume a more important role. Bowlan, in particular, has impressed with his high-90s fastball and consistent strike-throwing. He was often shuttled back and forth between the majors and minors while with the Kansas City Royals before joining the Phillies in an offseason trade.

They are going to keep testing his resolve.

“His stuff has been good and he’s performing,” Mattingly said. “Bullpens, you always go into the season with some idea who’s your ninth-inning guy, who are your setup guys and things like that. But, for me, bullpens always set themselves because the guys that are pitching well get the ball. And who’s throwing the ball the best gets the ball the most. That’s just the way it works, and that’s what he’s been doing.”

The Phillies entered the final 65 games with a bullpen that grades well in underlying measurements. It has improved a declining whiff rate from a season ago. It has MLB’s second-highest strikeout rate in 2026 and the seventh-lowest walk rate. It has allowed the third-weakest contact by average exit velocity.

But it ranks 22nd in ERA.

Getting the ball to Duran has been laborious at times. After Duran, Bowlan and Kerkering, who has sometimes struggled to throw strikes, these are the available righties: Max Lazar, Seth Johnson and Chase Shugart.

Internally, the team’s best bullpen prospect is Alex McFarlane. He is 25 and still at Double-A Reading, where he’s posted a 2.12 ERA in 34 innings. He’s carrying a 13 percent walk rate, which is high, but he’s struck out 33 percent of the batters he’s faced. He features a high-90s fastball with tantalizing stuff. He does not have polished command. The Phillies have no idea how he’d react to more stressful situations. They probably need to see soon.

McFarlane is expected to be promoted to Triple-A Lehigh Valley in the near future, according to two team sources who were not authorized to speak publicly.

In the weeks ahead, Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski will have to debate what is most pressing to address in a trade. The Phillies could use another outfielder, preferably one who bats right-handed. A fifth starter would help. But the bullpen situation might merit the most attention.

Last summer, the Phillies were in the market for the same items. They traded two top-rated prospects for Duran, who has excelled. They landed Harrison Bader as an outfield buttress.

The Phillies’ two biggest external additions from this past offseason — Keller and Adolis García — are sidelined. That leaves the front office trying to correct the same problems again.

Lacking prospect capital and having various needs could nudge the Phillies toward a measured approach that seeks several marginal upgrades. That is a tactic Dombrowski has often taken at the deadline, the Duran deal being an exception.

The Phillies’ opponent this weekend, the moribund New York Mets, could be their bullpen trade supplier. The Mets have two left-handed relievers, Brooks Raley and A.J. Minter, who will likely be traded at the deadline. The veterans are both free agents next offseason. They will not command a heavy prospect return, but there will be league-wide interest.

Luke Weaver, a righty setup man who signed for a two-year, $22 million deal, is having an exceptional season. Weaver has 43 strikeouts and 11 walks in 39 innings with a 1.85 ERA. The Mets could opt to keep Weaver for when they plan to contend again in 2027. Or they could sell high now.

Keller’s injury has potential implications beyond 2026. He said he will seek a second opinion with Keith Meister, a leading orthopedic surgeon based in Texas. Even an internal brace procedure, and not the full Tommy John surgery, would probably affect Keller’s availability in 2027.

The Keller situation is similar to one with David Robertson years ago; the Phillies signed him to a two-year, $23 million deal before the 2019 season, and he logged 6 2/3 innings before requiring Tommy John surgery. Even further back, another two-year deal to setup man Mike Adams was derailed by a significant shoulder injury.

Predicting relievers is difficult. The Phillies were burned by one-year deals to Jordan Romano and Joe Ross last season. They took a bigger swing with Keller. But they’re back in the same spot: Feeling a little short in a bullpen that has disappointed them in each of the last three Octobers.

Over the next few weeks leading up to training camp, we’ll be counting down the top 25 most important Eagles for the 2026 season.

He’s 36 now and entering Year 14 in the NFL. But when he’s healthy, there aren’t many players in the NFL who are better than Lane Johnson.

He’s a future Hall of Famer who hasn’t lost a step yet. The Eagles need that to continue in 2026.

Last season, Johnson was playing at a familiarly high level until he suffered a Lisfranc injury in November. The plan was for Johnson to eventually return and that was the hope even into the playoffs. But ahead of the playoff game against the 49ers, Johnson’s foot swelled again and he wasn’t able to go.

While Johnson is at the age where he considers retirement after every season, he actually wasn’t very close to hanging up his cleats this offseason.

“I didn’t want to go out that way,” Johnson explained this spring.

NFL

Johnson said last month that he was feeling healthy again.

“I’ve been able to play through stuff throughout the years but this was just something that took time,” Johnson said. “That’s something that I didn’t have at that point of the season. It was probably around February, March when I started to feel 100% but it took some time for it to heal up. I didn’t want to go out on that note last year.”

If you need more proof that Johnson is supremely important to the Eagles — and you probably don’t — you can always just look at the records. Here’s how the Eagles have fared with and without Johnson since the start of the 2016 season (including playoffs):

With Johnson: 94-41-1

Without Johnson: 15-28

In the first 13 seasons of his career, Johnson played for just one offensive line coach, so it’s a big change for him now that Jeff Stoutland is no longer with the organization. While that news was an initial shock for Johnson this offseason, he has bought into the new offense being implemented by offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and seems legitimately excited about it.

“Hey man, I’m about it,” Johnson said. “Coach (Chris) Kuper played for lots of years in the league. Not only coming to me as a coach but as a player, I have a lot of respect for him. Super smart. I just think how this offense here will help us. I think just stretching the field, stressing the defense more. I think it’ll help us with our run blocking angles. I think it’ll help us some in pass pro.

“I’ve never had any guard help all these years. It’s always been 1-on-1 so having the ability to be inside and having the guard come out and help me is a big deal for me. Me likey. Very excited. That’s pretty cool.”

text:
Fantasy football is a year-round obsession for some of us, but plenty of managers only flip the engine back on in the middle of July. We are a week or two from training camp, before the flood of daily practice reports, tweaks, and setbacks begins. Right now is the calm before that storm; a perfect window to catch up on the injuries already shaping the 2026 season. Here is where every notable name stands as camps open.

Rashee Rice, WR, Kansas City Chiefs

Let’s separate the two storylines here, because only one of them touches your lineup. Rashee Rice has real off-field concerns, headlined by a 30-day jail stint. I am not going to pretend that noise does not exist. On the field, though, the news is clean.

Advertisement

Rice had a cleanup procedure on the knee where he tore his LCL back in 2024. It is fair to wonder how hard he attacked the rehab with everything else going on, but the surgery itself is not expected to slow him at all. He should be a full go when Kansas City Chiefs camp opens.

Josh Allen, QB, Buffalo Bills

File this one under much ado about nothing. Josh Allen broke a bone in his foot in Week 16 last season and, being who he is, played right through it. He had surgery to repair it in January and was a full participant by OTAs. There is no fantasy concern here whatsoever.

Malik Nabers, WR, New York Giants

This is the one that worries me. Malik Nabers tore both his ACL and his meniscus in Week 4 last season. That pairing is far more complicated than a clean ACL. His recovery has not been smooth, either. He needed a second procedure in May to clear out scar tissue that was stalling his progress. The party line was that the cleanup would not affect his timeline, but that is not how bodies work. Any time a surgeon goes back into a joint, it is a fresh issue that demands its own recovery.

Advertisement

START PREPARING: PFN’s Fantasy Mock Draft Simulator

The vibes have not been good. New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has stopped short of ruling Nabers out for Week 1, but the plugged-in beat reporters, Jordan Raanan among them, are pointing toward Nabers missing at least the first month. Do not be surprised if he opens the year on the PUP list.

That fallout lands hardest on Jaxson Dart, who now faces an even leaner situation than the one he inherited last year with Wan’Dale Robinson around. Until Nabers is back, Darius Slayton and Darnell Mooney project as the top wideouts, so expect Dart to lean heavily on free-agent tight end Isaiah Likely.

Cam Skattebo, RB, New York Giants

The news out of the other side of the Giants’ offense is far more encouraging. Cam Skattebo suffered a gruesome ankle fracture in Week 8, but every report on his rehab has been positive, a stark contrast to the Nabers situation down the hall. He is at no real risk of missing Week 1 and should be practicing early in camp.

Advertisement

The one caveat is the nature of the injury itself, which could sap a little of his burst and explosion early in the year. We might see a bit more Tyrone Tracy in September as a result, but I still expect Skattebo to start Week 1.

Quinshon Judkins, RB, Cleveland Browns

Quinshon Judkins is another back coming off a lower-leg injury, having broken his fibula very late in the year in Week 16. The key detail is that there was no structural damage, which made his recovery far more straightforward.

This was a milder version of what Tony Pollard and Isiah Pacheco dealt with, though both of those backs saw the injury quietly drain their explosiveness the next season. That is the fear with any fibula break.

Advertisement

Judkins is doing his best to erase those concerns. He participated at OTAs and looked much better than anyone expected, pushing off the injured leg without hesitation. And that was in the Spring. By the time Cleveland Browns camp opens, and certainly by Week 1, he should have full trust in the leg. I am cautiously optimistic this ends up a non-factor in 2026.

Bucky Irving, RB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

It was a lost season for Bucky Irving in 2025. A minor foot injury in Week 4 cleared up in about two weeks, but a shoulder problem he revealed later cost him time all the way until Week 13.

The truth is the shoulder was never fully right at any point last year. Irving had surgery to fix it this offseason. Head coach Todd Bowles floated a bizarre timeline of Irving being ready “in August or September,” which turned out to be nonsense, as Irving practiced at OTAs and should have no trouble being ready for camp well ahead of Week 1.

Advertisement

For the record, Irving is still my No. 1 running back fade in fantasy this year, but that has almost nothing to do with the injury.

Rome Odunze, WR, Chicago Bears

Rome Odunze is not actually injured, but he said something this offseason worth filing away. Odunze admitted he is adjusting to a “new normal” with his foot after playing through a stress fracture last season, which he probably should not have done.

DIVE IN: PFN’s Fantasy Football HQ

The bone healed in a way that leaves the foot feeling different to him. By his own account, it should not hinder his play, though it is something he is still getting used to. I would not let it change how I value him in fantasy.

Advertisement

Alec Pierce, WR, Indianapolis Colts

Alec Pierce is a name to monitor closely. He underwent ankle surgery this offseason that was significant enough that he is not a lock to be ready when camp opens. Pierce should be fine for Week 1, but I would keep an eye on whether the ankle nags him once the games count.

The stakes are higher for his role now, because with Michael Pittman Jr. gone, Pierce has no competition for the Indianapolis Colts’ primary X receiver. If the surgery lingers into the season, Josh Downs would be the clear beneficiary of extra volume.

Tucker Kraft, TE, Green Bay Packers

Tucker Kraft tore his ACL in Week 8 last season. By every account, the rehab is going exceptionally well. He is on track to suit up in Week 1 for the Green Bay Packers. There is a decent chance he does not feel fully like his old self until late in the season or even 2027, since that is how ACLs tend to go. Even so, a healthy-enough Kraft at his current price looks like one of the better tight end values on the board.

Advertisement

Patrick Mahomes, QB, Kansas City Chiefs

Here is the big one. Patrick Mahomes tore his ACL in Week 15 last season. History is not kind to late-season ACL tears when it comes to being ready for the start of the following season. Mahomes, of course, is not a normal case. The man is obsessed with football and has attacked this rehab as aggressively as humanly possible. Every report has been positive. The expectation is that he suits up in Week 1. Justin Fields sits behind him as the backup, which matters only if something changes.

Xavier Worthy, WR, Kansas City Chiefs

Xavier Worthy’s season got off to a brutal start in Week 1 last year, when Travis Kelce accidentally rammed into him on a crossing route and left him with a dislocated shoulder and a torn labrum. He only missed two weeks, but Andy Reid later admitted the team had to trim his route tree the rest of the way to protect the shoulder.

Advertisement

Worthy had surgery in January to clean it up and is finally back to 100%. His talent and long-term upside are a fair debate, but his health is not something I would sweat heading into drafts.

Sam LaPorta, TE, Detroit Lions

Sam LaPorta’s 2025 season ended after Week 10 because of a back injury. Back issues always make me nervous, and this was a significant one. The good news is that he had surgery to address it and is fully expected to be ready when Detroit Lions camp opens. I want to see him moving well before I get too comfortable, but the baseline expectation is a normal ramp-up.

Jonathon Brooks, RB, Carolina Panthers

Jonathon Brooks is heading into his third NFL season having barely stepped on the field. He spent his rookie year rehabbing a torn ACL, then retore it just three games into his comeback.

Advertisement

STAY UPDATED: PFN’s Fantasy News Tracker

Brooks missed all of 2025 recovering, but the reports this offseason have been encouraging. If the knee holds and the burst returns, it is well within reason that Brooks overtakes Chuba Hubbard as the Carolina Panthers’ lead back at some point this season.

Bo Nix, QB, Denver Broncos

Bo Nix broke his ankle in the AFC Divisional Round, an injury that forced the Denver Broncos to hand the ball to Jarrett Stidham in the AFC Championship Game. Some recent pictures of the ankle made the rounds and raised a few eyebrows this offseason. Even so, Nix is expected to be a full go for training camp. I am not sounding any alarms yet, though it is worth tracking how the ankle looks once he is moving at full speed.

Advertisement

George Kittle, TE, San Francisco 49ers

George Kittle tore his Achilles in the final game of 2025, which is about the last injury you want to see for a 33-year-old whose game runs on explosiveness. Here is why I am not writing him off. Kittle carries the same maniacal, in-the-best-way obsession that Mahomes does. He has always been a notably fast healer, and the tear happened in a fortuitous spot that has sped up his timeline. He is tracking to play in September, even if that lands a week or two after the opener.

Plan accordingly at the position. Jake Tonges would step into the starting San Francisco 49ers tight end job and profiles as a perfectly viable streamer for as long as Kittle is sidelined.

Chris Rodriguez, RB, Jacksonville Jaguars

The Jacksonville Jaguars brought in Chris Rodriguez to be their between-the-tackles power back, but a foot injury has kept him out of OTAs so far. That is not ideal timing, since it puts CRod behind the eight ball in his competition with Bhayshul Tuten for touches.

Advertisement

Rodriguez is still expected to be ready for training camp, so there is time to make up ground. However, this shakes out, the Jaguars’ backfield touch distribution remains one of the more fascinating puzzles in fantasy.

Daniel Jones, QB, Indianapolis Colts

Daniel Jones tore his Achilles in Week 14. His rehab is reportedly coming along well enough that he is expected to be ready for Week 1. I would pump the brakes on assuming he is all the way back, though. Achilles tears routinely take a full calendar year before a player looks like his old self.

The bigger wrinkle is that the tear was to his push-off foot, which is exactly the leg a quarterback drives from to throw deep. That gives me real pause about his ability to stretch the field early in the year, and is a concern for Pierce, whose game relies entirely on downfield passes.

text:
Fred Warner continues to set the standard at his position.

In ESPN's annual survey of NFL executives, coaches, and scouts, the San Francisco 49ers linebacker was voted the No. 1 off-ball linebacker in the league heading into the 2026 season. The rankings are based on over 70 league voters to highlight the best players at each position right now.

Warner, who also earned the No. 1 spot in last year's rankings, received almost 70 percent of the first-place votes. Despite appearing in just six games last season due to an ankle injury, Warner made an immediate impact whenever he was on the field. He finished the year with 51 tackles (two for loss), three passes defended, two forced fumbles, and one fumble recovery.

An NFL coordinator praised what separates Warner from the rest of the league.

"He diagnoses faster than anyone," the coordinator told ESPN. "That's really his secret sauce. Processes the game at an incredibly fast level."

“I would say they’re on schedule. Now, people hear that and say, ‘well, what does that mean?’ Well, I don’t really know,” Harbaugh said with a laugh. “Because nobody knows. [Skattebo] is further ahead based on the type of injury but Malik is not far behind. He’s in a good place right now.”

Nabers appeared at the Brian Burns Charity Softball Game on May 30 and was seen limping, causing many a Giants fan to worry about his progression.

“We were eight months in and he looked like that?!,” former Giants RB Tiki Barber said on WFAN this week. “He looked bad [at the softball game] … I’m doubtful that [Nabers] is going to be pain-free [in training camp], swelling-free, and fully viable for a good portion of training camp.”

Nabers tore his ACL and suffered meniscus damage on Sept. 28, 2025 in a game against the LA Chargers. During the second quarter, Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart threw a deep pass down the right sideline to Nabers. Nabers’ right leg bucked as he went up to try and make the grab. The star WR immediately grabbed his leg and had to be carted off the MetLife Stadium field.

Nabers waited a full month to have surgery, and at the time his camp said the delay would have no bearing on his return date. The Athletic later revealed that Nabers had to have a second surgery due to “knee stiffness” during his recovery. This second surgery was dubbed a “cleanup procedure” but has further put a delay on Nabers’ recovery timeline.

It typically takes 9-12 months for an NFL player to recover from ACL surgery and be ready to play. One recent example of an NFL receiver bouncing back from an ACL tear rather quickly is Stefon Diggs.

Diggs had surgery in October 2024 but was able to be a full participant in New England Patriots training camp the next summer. The veteran did not play in any of the Patriots’ preseason games but was ready to go in Week 1 of the 2025 regular season.

It is highly unlikely that Nabers will play in any of the Giants’ preseason games, and Week 1 of the regular season is still very much in the air. There is also the very real possibility that the Giants place Nabers on injured reserve to start the season, which means he would not be eligible to play until Week 5 of the regular season.

If he undergoes surgery on his right elbow, it would keep him out a significant portion, if not all, of 2027 as well, Passan reports.

MORE: Phillies announce death of former All-Star closer at 73

The Phillies signed Keller to a two-year contract in December 2025. He is owed $7 million this season and $11 million next year.

In his career with the Kansas City Royals (2018-23), Chicago White Sox (2024), Boston Red Sox (2024), Chicago Cubs (2025) and Phillies, Keller is 44-60 with a 4.13 ERA.

Keller found his stride last year as a set-up man for the Cubs. He finished the season 4-2 with a 2.07 ERA across 68 appearances, striking out 75 batters in 69.2 innings.

That set him up for a strong payday in his free agent walk year. His conversion to a max-effort relief pitcher, along with his usage, might also have set him up for a major injury.

If Keller needs Tommy John surgery, he will be expected to miss the next 12 to 18 months.

With the MLB trade deadline looming on Aug. 3, the Phillies just became major players to acquire relief help. In the meantime, right-handers Orion Kerkering, Jonathan Bowlan, and Chase Shugart figure to move up the bullpen pecking order.

text:
Death, taxes and the NFC North being competitive.

It seems Minnesota's division every season has at least two or three teams vying for the top position — and sometimes two or three teams making their way into the playoffs.

NFL.com's Nick Shook recently ranked all eight of the league's divisions and topped his list with the NFC North. He noted while "the biggest question mark resided in Chicago" this time last year, the Bears will enter the 2026 campaign "as the reigning division champion with enough optimism to build a skyscraper taller than the Willis Tower." Shook wrote:

Ben Johnson is coming off a fantastic debut season as head coach. Quarterback Caleb Williams is on the cover of Madden NFL 27. Super Bowl LX Champion Coby Bryant hopped on the bandwagon via a three-year, $40 million free-agent deal. Even if the Bears know the heart-stopping style with which they won a significant portion of their 2025 games is unsustainable, everything is looking up in the Windy City.

But Shook warned to not overlook the rest of the division, including the Vikings. He said Minnesota "has spent the entire offseason playing the 'What If' game," but if the Vikings find stability at the quarterback position, they "should be primed for a legit playoff run."

In Detroit, the Lions are looking to rebound from a 9-8 season with the help of new Offensive Coordinator Drew Petzing, who spent 2014-19 as an assistant coach with the Vikings.

Detroit won't be caught by surprise in the trenches this season, not after adding center Cade Mays to solve the issues in the interior, then signing Larry Borom and Ben Bartch as depth additions and acquiring Juice Scruggs in a deal that sent David Montgomery to Houston. Yes, this is now Jahmyr Gibbs' backfield, and hopefully, the offseason efforts are enough to get the ground game back on track. Three new defensive backs — Roger McCreary, Chuck Clark and Christian Izien — should bring the same needed depth to that side of the ball.

Shook evaluated Green Bay, noting Head Coach Matt LaFleur "willingly reset" the Packers offense and changed up the receiving corps.

It's a necessary refresh for a team that admittedly felt stale in 2025 and repeatedly failed to deliver in the biggest late-season moments (at Denver, plus two losses in Chicago). The talent remains … but the trust isn't quite there for the Packers as of now. That can change quickly.

When all is said and done? The NFC North looks poised for another close race.

At the outset of last season, three of the four member clubs were seen as legitimate threats to win the NFC North and embark on Super Bowl pursuits. The one team most didn't take seriously ended up winning the division. A battle royale awaits in the North.

Check out Shook's full division rankings here.

ESPN ranks Justin Jefferson No. 2 among WRs

ESPN's Jeremy Fowler is once again rolling out positional rankings after talking to NFL executives, coaches and scouts. He explained:

Here's how it works: Voters gave their own top 10 players at a position, then we compiled the results and ranked candidates based on the number of top-10 votes, composite average and dozens of interviews, with research and film study help from ESPN NFL analyst Matt Bowen as well as ESPN Research.

In the wide receiver rankings, Justin Jefferson once again landed at No. 2 behind — just barely behind — his former LSU teammate Ja'Marr Chase. Fowler noted Jefferson "registered No. 1 or No. 2 votes on around 70% of the ballots, with several voters considering him a cut above the rest."

An unnamed AFC executive told Fowler Jefferson is "a proven commodity that can do everything you need and can adapt to any defensive look."

An NFC executive said choosing between Jefferson and Chase is a tough task.

"Chase vs. Jefferson is still kind of like Bijan [Robinson] and [Jahmyr] Gibbs at running back — almost like 1 and 1A," he told Fowler. "Maybe a little more big-play ability with Jefferson."

Jefferson's 8,480 receiving yards are the most for any player in his first six seasons in NFL history. His six straight 1,000-yard campaigns tie Randy Moss for second in franchise history (Cris Carter is first with eight).

Jefferson's career-low 1,048 yards in 2025 hurt his vote share slightly, but most voters gave him a pass due to poor quarterback play. And several voters noted how professionally Jefferson handled the offense stalling. His 53.4% double-team percentage ranked first among receivers, and he eclipsed 1,500 yards the previous season with Sam Darnold.

Fowler finished his recap of Jefferson by referencing a coach's comments about the Vikings receiver:

Forget the 50-50 catch. Jefferson can make 20-80 catches, an NFL coordinator said. "That catch he made in Buffalo [in 2022], I don't think Chase makes that."

text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- Syracuse quarterback Steve Angeli said he's fully recovered from the Achilles tendon injury that cost him most of the 2025 season.

Angeli sustained the injury to his left leg in Syracuse's fourth game, at Clemson, following a blistering start where he threw for 1,316 yards -- second most in the FBS at the time -- and 10 touchdowns. He underwent season-ending surgery and began a long rehab process.

Angeli said he first felt 100% several weeks ago.

"The athletic training staff, coach Fran [Brown] and our strength staff have done a good job of keeping me on a load management plan throughout all the recovery," Angeli told ESPN. "And as we get into practice, still being able to monitor it, but starting to ramp everything up to be able to be full-go for the season and just doing it smartly."

Angeli transferred to Syracuse in 2025 after several years as a reserve at Notre Dame, which included a College Football Playoff appearance.

He earned the Syracuse starting job during training camp and will enter the fall as QB1, ahead of a group full of new talent as Syracuse added quarterback transfers Amari Odom (Kennesaw State) and Malachi Nelson (UTEP), the former No. 1 overall national recruit.

Although Syracuse beat Clemson to improve to 3-1, the team lost its final eight games, all by 13 points or more. Defensive back/wide receiver Demetres Samuel Jr. admitted that several players "lost a bit of confidence when Steve went down."

"When I got hurt, I remember, you know, being on the sideline and talking to our pastor and talking to my mom and just being like, 'Why God? Like, what did I do?'" Angeli said. "It's one of those moments where it's a little emotional talking about it now because sometimes there's not an answer for it, but as I've gone through everything, I've just learned a lot about myself. It's just tough when you watch the way the rest of the season goes. ... I tried to do everything I could, obviously unable to physically, but it is definitely rough and definitely sucks."

Angeli participated in the Manning Passing Academy last month in Louisiana and won't have any restrictions or fear of reinjury when Syracuse begins preseason camp.

"I feel great, and I feel even better than I did before," he said.
